html:
On Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's in Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as emperor of the Romans. It was the first time in over three centuries that the West had an emperor.

Charlemagne had spread the Frankish kingdom across most of Western Europe: he conquered the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons in long brutal wars, and the Avars. In 799 Roman nobles attacked Leo, who fled to Charlemagne for help, and Charlemagne restored him. The crowning followed. His biographer Einhard claimed he would not have entered the church had he known, but historians doubt it.

In Constantinople the throne was held by a woman, Irene, so the West could argue that the imperial seat was empty. Byzantium saw the crowning as a theft of its title and accepted it, in a limited form, only in 812. The idea of a Western emperor crowned by the pope lived on in the Holy Roman Empire until 1806. The alliance of pope and Franks went back to the baptism of Clovis.
sum: On Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's in Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as emperor of the Romans. It was the first time in over three centuries that the West had an emperor.
